column1: # Evidence behind CREDITS.md. One row per tracked file. Validated by scripts/check-provenance.sh.
# Keep that pin on its own line. --online reads the ECU commit with `grep -m1 '^# ecu=' | sed
# 's/.*(\([0-9a-f]\{40\}\)).*/\1/'`, and that leading `.*` is greedy: a second 40-hex parenthesis on
# the ecu= line wins, so --online clones ECU and tries to check out a Superpowers SHA that is not in
# that clone — git errors and the script dies under set -e. Measured. Guarded in
# tests/test-provenance-origins.sh, which nothing else would catch: no test runs --online.
# NOTE: README/LICENSE/CONTRIBUTING/CLAUDE.md/.gitignore share a path with ECU but are ours, not vendored.

anchored destructive-verb patterns to command position (start-of-line or after ;/&&/||/|) and bounded the verb-to-path gap to the same command segment, so text merely co-occurring with a path (JSON argument, unrelated chained command) no longer misclassifies as a destructive write (Defect 6); corrected the retry-affordance message to state byte-identical retry and print the recorded key (Defect 7); hardens echo|grep -q pipe against pipefail SIGPIPE fail-open on large content (here-string); 2026-08-13 surface-criterion O2: the five substring-anywhere patterns anchored or re-grounded so the gate stops blocking prose about a destructive command -- the three git verbs given the file's own CMD_START (plus the git -C/-c option forms, which were a false negative); find split out of the .meta deletion alternation and made to require an actual deletion action, since find alone lists; destructive SQL made to require a database client to be named, because CMD_START on SQL would have switched the classification off entirely; the C# member expression dropped as something no shell command position can hold, replaced by the two shapes that erase preferences from a shell; review round 1: the find clause required a deletion verb only, so the find route to a mass .meta RENAME went from blocked to allowed while this file's header and HOOK-REFERENCE.md both promise deletion or rename -- rename restored, and the verb now matched as a token so a path prefix, a git wrapper or a quote before it no longer hides it; git's global option forms extended past -c/-C, closing --git-dir; the closed-allowlist limit of the SQL client check and the macOS plist misclassification both named in comments rather than left to be rediscovered; re-review: restoring one rename verb restored one verb out of a family -- the find action arms now enumerate deletion (rm, unlink, shred, truncate) and rename (mv, rename, prename, mmv) instead of a single token each. Before this wave ANY find naming .meta was classified, which is why a count was blocked and also why every destructive verb was covered for free; requiring an action gave back the counts and dropped six acts with them, each measured blocked at be2a582 and allowed after. An enumerated verb list is a claim about what someone thought of, and that is recorded in the file rather than left implied; round 3 -- the find route stops enumerating harm. A hand-written denylist of destructive verbs was written three times and was incomplete every time; the decisive miss was perl-rename / file-rename, the same tool as prename under its other standard names, hidden by the same left-boundary mechanism the comment above it explained. The find shape is now decided by an ALLOWLIST of read-only commands: keep the action requirement (a count and a bare -print still pass), and once there is an exec'd command classify unless that command cannot modify what find hands it. The command is extracted by tokenising in bash rather than by regex, because the word after the introducer is a position and the regex attempts to express it are what kept missing verbs. One classification, meta-mutation, naming the command it saw rather than guessing deletion or rename -- the decision no longer depends on knowing the verb, so the message must not claim to. The direct shape stays a denylist by ruling, since anything at all can name a path, and is widened to the verbs known today; it is incomplete by construction; round 4, the same defect class a third time: the want-branch skip list carried a backslash-prefix arm meant for find's own terminator and it skipped EVERY token beginning with a backslash, so the standard alias-bypass spellings were invisible on the find route -- the escaped rm and mv were permitted outright, and an escaped mv into a directory still blocked but reported the DIRECTORY as the command it had seen, having skipped both the verb and the placeholder. The terminator is now matched in full and a leading backslash is stripped from every token before anything looks at it, which also restores an escaped xargs as an introducer; CMD_START gained the same optional backslash, closing five measured false negatives on the direct arm (Library wipe, .meta deletion, .meta rename, find, and the hard reset), all of which were permitted before. Separately, an xargs option's mandatory separate ARGUMENT was being read as the command, so a read-only pipeline blocked and named a number as the verb; only options whose argument is mandatory and separate are skipped, because -i/-e/-l take an optional ATTACHED one and skipping their next word would step over the real command. Allowlist: du, b2sum, sha512sum, identify and the bracket form of test added; touch REMOVED, since mtime is a Unity reimport trigger; sort moved to a second stage, since its -o form is the documented in-place rewrite; dos2unix proposed and refused, because its man page states old-file mode overwrites the input and is the default, so listing it would sanction a mass rewrite. A five-arm second stage now covers commands that are read-only in the form you meet them and destructive in one other: sed/gsed/yq on an in-place flag, sort/openssl on an output flag, awk/gawk/mawk on a redirect or system(), and git on a read-only subcommand list. Each arm reads the haystack in which being WRONG BLOCKS rather than permits -- the flag arms read the whole command line, git reads only the token straight after itself, so an unrelated later read-only git cannot vouch for an earlier destructive one. The message now says the command is not on THIS GATE'S read-only list rather than that it is not read-only, which for git log was simply false; and meta-mutation, the one classification that asserts nothing about the act, gets its own shorter demand instead of asking for a rollback plan for what may be a read.; round 5: that second stage decided its flag by regexing the WHOLE RAW COMMAND with a right boundary of space/equals/dot/end, and shell quoting walked straight past it -- ten spellings that rewrite every .meta they are handed were permitted, including the canonical cross-platform form with an empty quoted suffix, the attached-suffix forms, the quoted flag itself, and gawk's in-place extension given as a separate pair; five were verified against real files with GNU sed 4.9 and gawk 5.2.1, and round 3 had blocked all ten because it had no second stage at all. It is this task's own defect class one level up: a token judged by its SHAPE in a wide haystack instead of by the POSITION it occupies, thrown away by a function that was already holding the tokenised argument list. The tokeniser now emits each exec'd command together with its OWN argument tokens, dequoted and bounded by its clause -- find's terminator, a shell operator, or the next introducer -- and the four arms read only those. That single narrowing closes the ten spellings and four false positives with them: a later grep -i or an xargs -i read as sed's flag, a shell redirect after the clause read as awk's, find's own -o read as sort's, and git's subcommand lost behind a global option that takes its own argument. The negative condition is preserved, so there is still no vouching direction and an unrecognised spelling costs a block rather than a pass. It also removes a cost: at 500 exec groups the classification went 264 ms to 148 ms, and with 120 KB of trailing text 2239 ms to 245 ms. The larger half of that was not the per-clause work at all but bash parameter-expansion on a very long token -- measured on this host, one such expansion on a 122880-character token costs 432 ms and the five dequoting steps cost 2098 ms, while a case against the same token costs 3 to 4 ms -- so the dequoting is now guarded by a case that fires only when the token actually starts with a backslash or a quote or ends with one, which is exact rather than a length cap. Known residual, narrower than what it replaces and awk-only: an xargs pipeline has no terminator token, so a trailing shell redirect lands among the exec'd command's arguments and blocks once.
